title: What Just 10 Minutes of Internet a Week Taught Me About Studying September 1, 2026
author: William Meller
summary: William Meller uses a childhood memory of having only ten minutes of internet access a week to introduce Dunlosky, Rawson, Marsh, Nathan and Willingham's landmark 2013 review of ten study techniques, and a 2021 Donoghue and Hattie meta-analysis that confirms its rankings. He walks through why the most commonly used study habits -- highlighting, rereading, and summarizing -- rate as low utility, while retrieval practice and distributed (spaced) practice rate as high utility despite being far less popular. Meller connects this to Robert Bjork's concept of 'desirable difficulty': techniques that feel easy, like rereading, create a false sense of familiarity that the brain mistakes for real mastery, while techniques that feel hard, like closed-book recall, actually build durable memory. He extends the argument past the classroom, noting that adults who read broadly but are never tested on the material face the same problem without the forcing function of an exam, and describes his own scarcity-driven childhood study method as an accidental version of spaced retrieval practice. The piece is part memoir, part research synthesis, aimed at both teachers and lifelong learners.
points: Summarizes the Dunlosky et al. (2013) review that sorted ten common study techniques into low, moderate, and high utility bands based on decades of experimental evidence.

Identifies the techniques most people actually use -- highlighting, rereading, and summarizing -- as the ones with the weakest evidence base, while retrieval practice and distributed practice rank highest but are underused.
Cites a 2021 Donoghue and Hattie meta-analysis (242 studies, over 169,000 participants) that reproduces the same ranking eight years later with an independent method.
Applies Robert Bjork's 'desirable difficulty' concept to explain why rereading feels productive (fluency mistaken for mastery) while retrieval practice feels uncomfortable but works better.

Extends the argument beyond students to adult lifelong learners, arguing that without an externally imposed exam, people must deliberately build their own retrieval tests or lose most of what they read.
quotes: In 2013, John Dunlosky, Katherine Rawson, Elizabeth Marsh, Mitchell Nathan and Daniel Willingham published a large review of study techniques in Psychological Science in the Public Interest. They took ten common techniques, the kind anyone can use alone, without a teacher and without special material, and tested each one against decades of experimental evidence.
Look at the low-utility list again. Highlighting. Rereading. Summarizing. That is basically the complete manual for how everyone studies.
Highlighting is, by a wide margin, the most universal thing in adult study. Yellow marker, pen, a finger dragging across the Kindle. And the measured benefit is minimal.

In 2021, Gregory Donoghue and John Hattie published a meta-analysis in Frontiers in Education on the same ten techniques. It covers 242 studies, 1,619 effects, 169,179 participants, with an overall mean of 0.56. The two most effective were still distributed practice and retrieval practice.

Robert Bjork calls this a desirable difficulty, the idea that the conditions making study easier in the moment are often the ones leaving memory weaker later. The reverse holds too. The effort that bothers you now is what sticks.

An adult reading a management book at eleven at night has no exam. Nobody will ask. Nobody will check. You can finish three hundred books without ever needing to remember a single paragraph, and life goes on exactly the same.
